detail.body:
Fixes #8828

## Summary
For hidden sizes <= 128 the inference norm launchers pack `256 / threadsPerGroup` rows into one thread block, but the kernels had no row bound. When `rows` is larger than that and not a multiple of it, the last block read its inputs and wrote its outputs for rows past the end of the tensors (e.g. fp32 hidden 64 or fp16/bf16 hidden 128 with 17 or 33 rows; see #8828).

This PR passes `rows` to `fused_ln`, `fused_residual_ln` (used by both residual launchers) and `rms_norm` / `pre_rms_norm`, computes the row index from the same expression the kernels already use for `block_offset`, and masks the global loads and stores of rows past the end. Those threads still take part in the reductions (masked loads return zeros), so the warp/block reductions are unchanged; there is no early return. Launch shapes (grid/block) are unchanged, and the launch macros just pass `rows` through.

## Why this is not a duplicate
- #8828 is the issue for this bug; no open PR addresses it (checked `gh pr list --search "8828 in:body"` and searches for the launcher names).
- #8827 (fp32 hidden 65-128 launched no kernel) adds the missing 32-thread branch and launches it one row per block; it does not touch the other branches. #8743 (rows == 0) adds an early return in the same launchers. Both touch the same files, so whichever merges second may need a trivial rebase. #8827 currently launches its 32-thread branch one row per block because the kernels had no row bound; with this PR merged that branch could use the default multi-row launch, but it does not have to change.

## Tests
Hardware: 1x NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080 Laptop GPU (sm_120), driver 595.99.02, CUDA 12.8, torch 2.11.0+cu128, Python 3.12.3. `transformer_inference` JIT-built separately for master and this branch (`TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=12.0`, `MAX_JOBS=4`).

Test changes (`tests/unit/ops/transformer/inference/`):
- `test_layer_norm.py`, `test_rms_norm.py`: `seq_len` `[1, 128]` -> `[1, 17, 33, 128]` and `channels` gains `32, 64` in all five parametrizations, so fp32/fp16/bf16 at 4-, 8- and 16-thread sizes run with partially filled blocks.
- `test_layer_norm.py`: new `test_layer_norm_residual_cuda` calling the CUDA residual bindings directly (`_layer_norm_residual`, `layer_norm_residual_store_pre_ln_res`) for rows 17/33 at fp32 32/64, fp16 64/128 and bf16 128, since `LayerNormOp.layer_norm_residual*` are PyTorch implementations.

Commands (from `tests/`): `pytest -m inference_ops unit/ops/transformer/inference/test_layer_norm.py` and `... test_rms_norm.py`.

| | master (`5f266e2`) | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `test_layer_norm.py` | 8 failed, 1096 passed | 1104 passed |
| `test_rms_norm.py` | 360 passed | 360 passed |

The 8 failures on master are `test_layer_norm_residual_cuda[store_pre_ln_res=True]` at exactly the partially filled shapes (fp32 32 / rows 33, fp32 64 / rows 17 and 33, fp16 64 / rows 33, fp16 and bf16 128 / rows 17 and 33): the overrun of the normalized output lands in the adjacent `res_output`. The other new cases (including all of `test_rms_norm.py`) pass on master too even though they overrun, because the stray accesses happen to hit unused memory; the memcheck table below is what shows the overrun.

memcheck (`PYTORCH_NO_CUDA_MEMORY_CACHING=1 compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck --padding 65536`, one process per case, direct calls to the five bindings; number = invalid accesses reported, 0 = clean; rows 9/13/17/33):

Counts are for the first faulting launch in each process (the CUDA context is lost afterwards). For `layer_norm`, `_layer_norm_residual` and `rms_norm` the count is 240/248; for `layer_norm_residual_store_pre_ln_res` and `pre_rms_norm` it is 238/246.

| config (threads per row, rows per block) | master: rows 9 / 13 / 17 / 33 | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| fp32 H=32 (8, 32) | 0 / 0 / 0 / 248 or 246 (all 5 bindings) | 0 everywhere |
| fp32 H=64 (16, 16) | 0 / 0 / 240 or 238 / 240 or 238 | 0 everywhere |
| fp16 H=64 (8, 32) | 0 / 0 / 0 / 248 or 246 | 0 everywhere |
| fp16 H=128 (16, 16) | 0 / 0 / 240 or 238 / 240 or 238 | 0 everywhere |
| bf16 H=128 (16, 16) | 0 / 0 / 240 or 238 / 240 or 238 | 0 everywhere |
| fp32 H=96, 128 (32-thread case) | 0 (no kernel is launched on master, #8826) | 0 (still no kernel without #8827) |
| fp16 H=256 (> 128 path, 1 row per block; control) | 0 | 0 |

Speed (CUDA events, 50 warm-up calls, then 200 calls captured in one CUDA graph and replayed 30 times; median per-call GPU time, mean of two passes alternating master/this branch, fresh process per configuration):

| op | dtype, H | rows | master (us) | this PR (us) | change |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| layer_norm | fp16, 128 | 17 / 1024 / 4096 | 1.052 / 1.238 / 1.618 | 1.012 / 1.276 / 1.611 | -3.8% / +3.1% / -0.4% |
| layer_norm + residual | fp16, 128 | 17 / 1024 / 4096 | 1.140 / 1.389 / 1.905 | 1.104 / 1.379 / 1.890 | -3.2% / -0.7% / -0.8% |
| rms_norm | fp16, 128 | 17 / 1024 / 4096 | 0.951 / 1.063 / 1.494 | 0.901 / 1.085 / 1.491 | -5.3% / +2.1% / -0.2% |
| layer_norm | fp32, 64 | 17 / 1024 / 4096 | 1.002 / 1.115 / 1.555 | 0.956 / 1.152 / 1.554 | -4.5% / +3.3% / -0.0% |
| layer_norm + residual | fp32, 64 | 17 / 1024 / 4096 | 0.976 / 1.329 / 1.901 | 0.981 / 1.263 / 1.893 | +0.5% / -4.9% / -0.4% |
| rms_norm | fp32, 64 | 17 / 1024 / 4096 | 0.931 / 1.023 / 1.526 | 0.889 / 1.063 / 1.524 | -4.5% / +3.9% / -0.1% |

The two passes agreed to within 1% for every entry. The differences are within about +/-5% (at most ~0.04 us per call). At 1024 rows layer_norm and rms_norm are 2-4% slower in both passes, at 4096 rows the two are equal, and at 17 rows this branch is 3-5% faster. Called from Python (eager, including the binding and output allocation) every configuration takes 2.5-2.7 us on both branches, so the kernel-time differences are not visible at that level.

Compatibility matrix: only the inference (v1, kernel-injection) layer_norm/rms_norm CUDA kernels change. Validated: fp32/fp16/bf16 via the unit tests above and memcheck, on sm_120. Not applicable: ZeRO stages, offload, training. Not validated: other GPUs/architectures, ROCm, end-to-end model inference.

Formatting: `pre-commit run --files <changed files>` (yapf reformatted the new test once; all hooks pass afterwards, clang-format 23.1.1).

AI assistance was used to prepare this change (code, tests and this description). I reviewed every changed line and ran the tests above.

(Reminder for the committer: DeepSpeed requires DCO sign-off, `git commit -s`.)

 from typing import Tuple
 
+import pytest
 import torch
 from deepspeed.accelerator import get_accelerator
 
@@ -44,3 +45,39 @@ def allclose(x, y, tolerances: Tuple[int, int] = None):
     else:
         rtol, atol = tolerances
     return torch.allclose(x, y, rtol=rtol, atol=atol)
+
+
+CANARY_VALUE = 1000.0
+
+
+def run_with_output_canaries(op, out_numel, dtype, num_outputs=1, canary_numel=0):
+    """Run ``op``, which allocates ``num_outputs`` outputs of ``out_numel`` elements each, so that every
+    output is directly followed in memory by a canary tensor owned by the caller and filled with
+    ``CANARY_VALUE`` (finite, so that NaN written past the end is detected as well).
+
+    A kernel that writes past the end of an output overwrites its canary, which plain pytest can then
+    detect. The layout is made deterministic with a private caching-allocator pool: one placeholder
+    block per output, each followed by its canary; the placeholders are freed so that the outputs
+    allocated inside ``op`` reuse them (best fit, lowest address first). Returns (outputs, canaries).
+    """
+    if not hasattr(torch.cuda, "use_mem_pool"):  #ignore-cuda
+        pytest.skip("requires torch.cuda.MemPool")  #ignore-cuda
+    device = get_accelerator().current_device_name()
+    nbytes = out_numel * torch.empty((), dtype=dtype).element_size()
+    pool = torch.cuda.MemPool()  #ignore-cuda
+    with torch.cuda.use_mem_pool(pool):  #ignore-cuda
+        placeholders, canaries = [], []
+        for _ in range(num_outputs):
+            placeholders.append(torch.empty(out_numel, dtype=dtype, device=device))
+            canaries.append(torch.full((canary_numel, ), CANARY_VALUE, dtype=dtype, device=device))
+        expected_ptrs = [t.data_ptr() for t in placeholders]
+        del placeholders
+        outputs = op()
+    get_accelerator().synchronize()
+
+    output_list = list(outputs) if isinstance(outputs, (list, tuple)) else [outputs]
+    # The check is only meaningful if each output sits right in front of its canary.
+    assert [t.data_ptr() for t in output_list] == expected_ptrs, "outputs did not reuse the placeholder blocks"
+    for t, canary in zip(output_list, canaries):
+        assert 0 <= canary.data_ptr() - (t.data_ptr() + nbytes) < 512
+    return outputs, canaries

+@pytest.mark.inference_ops

+        assert (canary == CANARY_VALUE).all()

inline_comments.body:
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Guard the inference-v2 sibling kernels too**

Under inference-v2, `elems_per_row <= 128` with more than one packed block and a non-multiple row count (for example fp16 H=128 with 17 rows) still corrupts memory: I checked `deepspeed/inference/v2/kernels/core_ops/cuda_layer_norm/layer_norm_cuda.cu` and `deepspeed/inference/v2/kernels/core_ops/cuda_rms_norm/rms_norm_cuda.cu`, and their identical launchers create 16 groups in the final block but their kernels receive no `rows` value or guard, so row indices 17–31 load and store past the tensors. This is reachable through public `CUDARMSNorm`, including EXAONE4's per-head Q/K normalization in `model.py:101-130`; apply this guard to both sibling implementations and add v2 coverage rather than leaving the same production OOB in place.

AGENTS.md reference: [AGENTS.md:L19-L19](https://github.com/deepspeedai/DeepSpeed/blob/31b0247e757153fb5b200756cd09f63ba0b6672b/AGENTS.md#L19-L19)

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Make the small-shape tests detect the overrun**

On a normal pytest run, these added RMS shapes and the analogous base layer-norm shapes do not detect the defect being fixed: the tests only compare values inside the returned logical tensors, while the surplus groups write after those tensors, so the parent implementation passes all of these RMS cases unless it happens to corrupt another allocation (the reported baseline is 360/360). Consequently `fused_ln`, `rms_norm`, or `pre_rms_norm` can lose its `valid_row` guard while CI remains green; use a canary/guard allocation or a sanitizer-backed regression that reliably fails on the old kernels instead of only broadening the parameter matrix.

AGENTS.md reference: [AGENTS.md:L76-L76](https://github.com/deepspeedai/DeepSpeed/blob/31b0247e757153fb5b200756cd09f63ba0b6672b/AGENTS.md#L76-L76)

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

Confirmed: the inference-v2 core-op kernels have the same unguarded sub-block launch.
- Kernels: `rms_norm` / `pre_rms_norm` in `deepspeed/inference/v2/kernels/core_ops/cuda_rms_norm/rms_norm_cuda.cu`, and `fused_ln` / `fused_residual_ln` in `cuda_layer_norm/layer_norm_cuda.cu`.
- Overrun: for elems_per_row <= 128 they pack several rows per block with no row bound, so when rows > rows-per-block and is not a multiple of it, the last block reads and writes past the end.
- Reachability: through the public `CUDARMSNorm`, for example EXAONE4's per-head Q/K RMSNorm (`model_implementations/exaone4/model.py`). There, `channels = head_size` and Q/K are normalized as `[tokens * n_heads, head_size]`.
- Evidence on master (5f266e26): compute-sanitizer memcheck through `CUDARMSNorm` reports out-of-bounds accesses for fp16/bf16 hidden 128 at 17 and 33 rows, and for hidden 64 at 33 rows; 16 rows is clean.

This PR is intentionally limited to the v1 / kernel-injection kernels, so I'll keep the v2 kernels out of scope here and open a separate issue for them, with the same row-guard fix offered.

Agreed. The new seq_len/channels cases pass on master under plain pytest; only compute-sanitizer memcheck catches the overrun, and memcheck isn't part of the default CI.

I've added canary tests that fail under plain pytest:
- New tests: `test_layer_norm_no_write_past_last_row` and `test_rms_norm_no_write_past_last_row`.
- Helper: `run_with_output_canaries` in `inference_test_utils.py`.
- Coverage: all five bindings (`layer_norm`, `_layer_norm_residual`, `layer_norm_residual_store_pre_ln_res`, `rms_norm`, `pre_rms_norm`), rows 17 and 33, at fp32 hidden 32/64 and fp16/bf16 hidden 64/128.
- How it works:
  - The outputs are allocated inside the bindings, so the helper uses a private `torch.cuda.MemPool` to place each output directly in front of a caller-owned canary tensor filled with a finite sentinel (1000.0).
  - It asserts that the layout holds, and then that the canary is unchanged after the call.
  - The tests skip when `MemPool` isn't available.
